title: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm: Same Formula. Different Axis.

intro.before: Both subtract a mean, divide by a standard deviation and rescale with learned γ and β. What differs is
intro.after: , and that decides where each one works.

bullets.text: Each feature is normalized over all samples in the mini-batch
Keeps running mean and variance, so inference needs no batch
The CNN standard: ResNet puts one after almost every conv layer
Tiny batches give noisy statistics, and train and eval can drift
Each sample is normalized over its own features, on its own
Same computation in training and inference, with no running stats
The Transformer standard: BERT and GPT-2 use it in every block
In convolutional networks it usually trails BatchNorm on accuracy

chart.title: Same numbers, two different means
chart.caption: Rows are samples, columns are features (γ = 1, β = 0). The same 9 becomes 1.22 under BatchNorm and 1.36 under LayerNorm.

a: Training CNNs on images with healthy batch sizes
Batch statistics are stable across steps
You want to fold it into the conv weights for inference
b: Transformers, RNNs and other sequence models
Batches are small, uneven or a single sample
Inputs vary in length, like tokens in a sentence

principles.sub: Stable image batches favor BatchNorm; tokens and sequences favor LayerNorm.
Skip it at inference and batch stats quietly change your outputs.
With tiny batches, LayerNorm or GroupNorm stays stable.

quote.big: Same formula. The axis is the decision.
quote.small: Normalize across samples, or across features.
